newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Coffee rise due to misjudgment-expert.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Coffee rise due to misjudgment-expert.

text.p: The rise in world coffee prices to their highest levels in two decades may in part be the result of large roasting companies misjudging the market in a big way, an Australian coffee expert said on Friday.

Andy Simkin, past president of the Australian Tea and Coffee Traders Association (ATCTA), said that as a result there may be room for coffee price to soar even higher as the roasters are forced to pay top dollar for coffee.

"Some roasters appear to be a position where they were expecting the market to fall out of bed, and now all they see is an upside -- and that in the short term is going to drive prices further," Simkin, the ATCTA's spokesman, said in an interview.

A spectacular rally in coffee prices accelerated on Thursday to lift New York futures above US$3.00/pound for the first time in 20 years. Simkin said some big roasters had mistakingly expected that prices would have peaked months ago.
"If you were arguing about whether to be buying coffee in New York at US$1.60, $1.70 or $1.80 (per pound), and you didn't, that would now look like cheap coffee," Simkin said.
"I can't speak for all the roasters, but it looks like some have got on the worng side of the market," he said.
"In the last 48 hours this has been a big contributing factor to rising prices," he said.
A fundamental shortage of more sought-after Arabica beans could intensify if a drought was to occur in Brazil, the world's largest producer, as some are suggesting, Simkin said.
Simkin estimates such a scenario could propel coffee prices to around US$4.50/pound. An industry perception that supplies are drying up elsewhere are also underpinning prices, he said.
The drought-hit industry in Kenya has pushed up premiums over the New York price by as much as US$2.30 per pound from the typical 30 cents, he said.
"You've actually got an outright market price of US$3.00 plus $2.20 or $2.30 (per pound)," Simkin said.
"So now you're up to around US$5.30 for a green bean for the spot position," Simkin said.

An 18,000-tonne cargo of Kenyan coffee delvered to Australia costing A$80,000 in January now fetches nearly A$250,000, Simkin said. Simkin there was evidence to suggest a high level of selling of coffee among growers holding supplies.
"There's quite a bit of origin selling, but in places like Kenya and Colombia there's just not a lot of coffee there," Simkin said.
Research suggested that for every five percent increase in the price of coffee there was a one percent decline in consumption, Simkin said.
